pests.name: Spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Very tiny pests that thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions and cause fine speckling and webbing on leaves. Marigolds are especially prone to them in midsummer. Spray plants with water and keep them watered to discourage mites.
pests.note_seasoned: Marigold's most characteristic pest: stippling and fine webbing under hot, dry, dusty conditions, worst in midsummer and on stressed or container plants. Raise humidity around foliage with base watering and dislodge with water sprays; insecticidal soap or miticide for heavy infestations.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth and buds. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and the flowers draw ladybugs and hoverflies that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth and buds; usually held in check by the beneficials marigold flowers attract. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap if populations build.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: These chew ragged holes in leaves and young plants, especially in damp weather and on tender seedlings. Hand-pick at night, remove hiding spots, or use iron-phosphate bait.
pests.note_seasoned: Ragged feeding on young plants and lower foliage in damp conditions; marigold seedlings are a frequent target. Reduce mulch harborage, hand-pick at night, or use iron-phosphate bait.

pests.name: Japanese beetles
pests.note_beginner: Shiny copper-and-green beetles that chew flowers and leaves in early-to-midsummer. Hand-pick them into soapy water in the morning when they are sluggish.
pests.note_seasoned: Metallic beetles that feed on blooms and skeletonize foliage in early-to-midsummer. Hand-pick at dawn into soapy water; avoid pheromone traps, which concentrate beetles.

diseases.name: Botrytis blight (gray mold)
diseases.note_beginner: A fuzzy gray mold that rots flowers and buds in cool, damp, crowded conditions, especially on the big double African types whose dense blooms trap moisture. Space plants for airflow, water at the soil, and remove rotted flowers.
diseases.note_seasoned: The signature wet-weather disease of marigold (Botrytis cinerea), favored by humidity, crowding, and overhead wetness; the dense double African blooms are especially prone to rotting from the center. Manage culturally: full sun, generous spacing, base watering, and prompt removal of spent or rotted heads. Do not compost infected debris.

diseases.name: Leaf spots and powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: Brown or dark spots, or a white powdery film on leaves, more common in damp, humid weather and crowded plantings. Keep foliage dry, space plants out, and remove badly affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Foliar spotting and occasional powdery mildew under humidity and crowding, spread by overhead wetness and splash. Manage with base watering, spacing for airflow, morning irrigation if overhead is unavoidable, and sanitation of infected debris.

diseases.name: Root, stem, and crown rot (damping-off)
diseases.note_beginner: Wet, poorly drained soil rots roots and stem bases, and young seedlings can collapse at the soil line. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and wait for warm soil before sowing.
diseases.note_seasoned: Soilborne rots and seedling damping-off driven by overwatering, poor drainage, and cold wet soil at sowing; dwarf French types are prone to rotting if kept too wet. Prevent with well-drained soil, warm-soil sowing, and restrained watering rather than treatment.

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.note_beginner: A disease spread by leafhoppers that distorts and yellows growth and turns flowers green or deformed. There is no cure; remove and discard affected plants so it does not spread.
diseases.note_seasoned: A leafhopper-vectored phytoplasma causing chlorosis, distortion, and virescent (greened) blooms across the aster family. No cure; rogue out symptomatic plants promptly and manage leafhoppers and nearby weed reservoirs.
